articles.summary: This year, 52 graduates of the CNX Foundation’s Mentorship Academy committed to a next step: a job, an apprenticeship, or military service. On August 14, graduates gathered at PNC Park for Signing Day — the culmination of a program year spent touring job sites, meeting industry leaders, and building the professional network that turns an interest into an offer. These graduates are heading into roles with CNX, UPMC, Deep Well Services, BestPLUS, Sevita Health, apprenticeships with the building trades, and — for three graduates — into military service. Many of these paths require no four-year degree, a focus of the Academy, which is built around access to opportunity rather than a single prescribed path. The relationship doesn’t end at the signing table. The mentors, employers, and peers a student meets through the Academy stay part of their world after graduation, reflecting the CNX Foundation’s micro-TIL philosophy — tangible, impactful, local support defined by follow-through rather than a one-time gesture. That is Appalachia First in practice: regional employers investing in regional talent, and young people finding that the opportunity they were looking for was already here. articles.summary: The Mon Valley Independent recently highlighted CNX’s bat stewardship efforts at Monessen’s City Park, where employees installed a bat box to provide additional roosting habitat. The project brings together employee teamwork, wildlife conservation, and practical support for a local community. CNX employees built the seven-chamber box using Pennsylvania Game Commission plans and installed it September 4, along with three bluebird boxes. Constructed with a rough-cut hemlock interior and durable aluminum exterior, the bat box was placed in a location selected for adequate sunlight and clear access for bats. “The City Park installation is part of CNX’s broader bat stewardship effort to provide additional roosting habitat and help residents understand the importance of bats,” Daniel Bitz, CNX’s director of permitting, told the Independent. “The box offers an alternative to homes and attics, while supporting conservation efforts for bat populations affected by white nose syndrome.” Beyond providing habitat, the installation increases awareness of bats’ role in the ecosystem, including their consumption of insects. It also aims to reduce potential conflicts between bats and residents by providing another summer roosting option. CNX provides and installs bat boxes at no cost to community partners. The Monessen project reflects the company’s Appalachia First vision and micro-TIL approach to community investment: tangible, impactful and local. articles.summary: The energy workforce of the next decade is sitting in a classroom right now — in a shop class, in an auditorium with an HVAC system that works, in a cafeteria line where a student isn’t doing math on lunch debt. Preparing and inspiring that workforce — removing the obstacles that have nothing to do with how hard a student works — takes a lot of hands. Educators, school staff, PTAs, coaches, and families carry most of that weight. CNX’s role is to help fill the remaining gaps. CNX’s Mentorship Academy is the most visible way the company helps, but it isn’t the only one. Across the communities where CNX operates, employees and the CNX Foundation show up in smaller, more immediate ways that make a school year successful: supplies on the first day, a paid-off lunch account, a partner who’ll respond when a district calls. These small acts remove the daily friction that determines whether a kid stays engaged long enough to become the welder, lineman, or engineer the region will need. That work is hyper-local by design, and it’s happening right now as the new school year gets underway. In July, 400 totes of school supplies were provided to Hempfield Area School District in Westmoreland County as part of CNX’s ongoing school supply initiative. The initiative also featured a July backpack and school supply giveaway by CNX’s Virginia operations team (shown at top). The event provided 1,000 clear backpacks to the community, helping Tazewell County students adhere to new school safety policy requiring clear backpacks. CNX volunteers have also assembled hundreds of personal hygiene kits. These are being distributed at back-to-school events over the next several weeks. Cumulatively, across the 2025-2026 and 2026-2027 school years, CNX has provided $75,549 in school supplies. That includes providing 49,632 pencils, 6,480 rolls of paper towels, 5,088 boxes of tissues, 4,980 dry-erase markers, and 2,300 backpacks, among other essential supplies. These efforts pick up where last spring left off. As the 2025-2026 school year came to a close, CNX held end-of-year appreciation lunches for teachers and staff at River Valley Middle-High School, Jeannette High School, and Armstrong Junior-Senior High School. Clearing the balance CNX has also worked to remove a barrier that follows students from one year to the next: unpaid school lunch balances. CNX has eliminated nearly $130,000 in outstanding lunch debt across its communities since 2023 – clearing students’ accounts and allowing those families to start the new year without a balance carried over from the last one. It’s a straightforward intervention with an outsized effect — no student’s meal account should determine how they show up to class. Each of these efforts reflects CNX’s micro-TIL — Tangible, Impactful, Local — approach to community support. Rather than a large check to a broad cause, CNX directs support to specific schools, specific students, and specific needs in the counties where its employees live and work. Together, these commitments helped students close out the last school year strong and gave them what they need to get the 2026–2027 year underway. articles.summary: CNX Resources has announced the next evolution of Radical Transparency, its first-in-the-nation public-private environmental monitoring and disclosure collaboration with Governor Josh Shapiro and the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP). The program will now add continuous ambient gamma radiation monitoring at CNX’s unconventional well pads and certain produced water facilities, along with expanded public disclosure of radiation surveys on waste leaving its operating sites. From Air and Water to Radiation Since Governor Shapiro and CNX signed the historic Statement of Mutual Interest in November 2023, Radical Transparency has grown from a commitment to disclose air quality, water quality, and drilling chemicals on a 24/7 basis into the most intensive independent study of unconventional natural gas wells in the nation. The partnership has also helped inform DEP rulemaking requiring broader chemical disclosure across the industry. Today’s announcement extends that same standard of site-level, third-party-verified data to radiation monitoring — one of the four core components of the program, alongside air quality monitoring, water quality monitoring, and additive disclosure. Onterris, formerly Montrose Environmental Group, is the accredited third-party environmental services provider bringing this new data online. With decades of experience in scientific testing and regulatory compliance across air, water, and radiological monitoring, Onterris will apply the same independent rigor to CNX’s radiation protection data that Clean Air Engineering already applies to air quality monitoring under the program. The Next Data Points Under the expanded program, CNX will: Install continuous ambient gamma radiation monitoring at or near its unconventional well pads and certain produced water facilities, covering every phase of well pad development from drilling through production. Raw data will be collected by Onterris and provided to CNX and DEP simultaneously, with quality assurance and quality control performed under a dedicated QA/QC plan. Just like air and water data, the results will be shared with the public in real time on the CNX Radical Transparency website. Expand public disclosure of waste transportation radiation surveys, consistent with CNX’s Comprehensive Radiation Protection Plan (CRPP). CNX already surveys the radiation level of waste leaving its sites before disposal — it will now disclose that daily survey data publicly, updated monthly, from drilling through production. CNX also conducts semiannual desktop reviews and annual on-site inspections of every waste handling facility it approves to receive its waste. Facts, Not Guesswork “Radical Transparency was never meant to be a program with an end date — it’s how we intend to manage our business moving forward, providing the public and policymakers the data needed to make informed decisions about the nature of natural gas development in Pennsylvania, and that means it must continue expanding and growing into new areas,” said Alan Shepard, President and CEO of CNX. “Just as we’ve done with air and water quality, we’re going to put actual, site-level radiation data in front of the public and DEP rather than allow questionable studies and speculation to drive the narrative on this important issue. These are voluntary commitments that go beyond what any regulation requires of us, because our communities deserve real data, not guesswork, about the operations happening near where they and we live and work.” CNX notes that these commitments are voluntary and go beyond the company’s existing compliance obligations under state and federal law. As with the rest of the Radical Transparency program, the goal is to give communities, regulators, and elected officials direct access to site-level data and facts — rather than assumptions or modeling. Additional information on Radical Transparency, including live monitoring data, is available at cnx.com/sustainability-radical-transparency.
